INTEREST OF AMICI1
The National League of Cities (“NLC”), founded in
1924, is the oldest and largest organization representing
U.S. municipal governments. NLC works to strengthen
local leadership, influence federal policy, and drive
innovative solutions. In partnership with 49 state municipal
leagues, NLC advocates for over 19,000 cities, towns, and
villages where more than 218 million Americans live.
The International Municipal Lawyers Association
(“IMLA”) is the nation’s oldest and largest organization
devoted solely to local government law. A nonprofit,
nonpartisan, professional association, IMLA’s membership
comprises more than 2,500 local government entities,
including cities, counties, and subdivisions thereof, as
represented by their chief legal officers, state municipal
leagues, and individual attorneys. IMLA’s mission is
to advance the responsible development of municipal
law through education and advocacy by providing the
collective viewpoint of local governments around the
country on legal issues before the United States Supreme
Court, as well as state and federal appellate courts.
Amici have an acute interest in preserving the ability
of local governments to safeguard the health, safety, and
welfare of their citizenry.
1. No part of this brief was authored by any party’s counsel,
and no person or entity other than amici funded its preparation
or submission.

2
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The question presented is whether state and local
governments have the authority to ban AR-15s or
whether the Second Amendment guarantees an absolute
right to possess such firearms nationwide, untethered
from history and tradition and regardless of local
conditions and factors that justify these restrictions.
The question is not whether state and local governments
must ban these weapons. What makes sense in Cook
County, Illinois, a highly urbanized environment with
virtually no hunting and limited recreational shooting
opportunities, is quite different than what makes sense
in Atascosa County, Texas, a rural community reliant on
agriculture and ranching and ravaged by feral hogs. In
the former, community leaders could rightly decide that
an AR-15, which can easily spray more than one bullet
per second, is likely to cause harm via a mass shooting
event or an ambush on law enforcement. In the latter,
community leaders could view the use of AR-15s by private
landowners seeking to control the feral hog population that
causes hundreds of millions of dollars in damage in crop
loss and infrastructure damage as a positive benefit to the
community. In both cases, local community leaders make
that decision to advance the health, safety, and welfare
of their communities. And in either case, if community
members do not like their leaders’ choices, then the answer
lies at the ballot box.
That political accountability and local autonomy
is entirely consistent with the Second Amendment
and this Nation’s history and tradition of regulating
unusually dangerous weapons. AR-15 advocates argue
that commonality supersedes their unusually dangerous

3
nature—despite repeated tragedies with hundreds
of our fellow citizens being murdered in minutes and
the dangers to law enforcement these weapons pose.
Enhanced with readily-available mechanisms that
approach machine-gun like rates of fire and large
capacity magazines, the increasing lethality of AR-15s
puts impossible pressures on law enforcement as they
struggle to protect our communities from mass shooting
events and recklessly endangers all of us, whether in
school, on streets, at parades, in churches, or elsewhere.
Restraining every local government nationwide from
prohibiting semi-automatic weapons in their community
needlessly endangers our society and fails to account
for the harms local governments face when all-toofrequent mass shooting events occur. Because history
and tradition does not transform the Second Amendment
into an enabler of manifestly dangerous instrumentalities
in our communities, local government leaders are not
powerless to act. To the contrary, the Court’s foundational
Second Amendment holdings have repeatedly recognized
a continuing role for local government in fashioning
reasonable firearm safeguards. This Court should make
good on that recognition and affirm.
ARGUMENT
I. The Second Amendment does not impose a
nationwide guarantee that assault weapons can be
kept and borne everywhere.
State and local governments have the fundamental
duty “to protect [their] citizens and provide for the safety
and good order of society.” Panhandle E. Pipe Line Co.
v. State Highway Comm’n of Kansas , 294 U.S. 613, 622

4
(1935). To fulfill this responsibility, localities must be
empowered to address the hazards posed by unusually
dangerous weapons in their midst. Considering the
substantial risk assault weapons pose to public safety,
Amici urge this Court to recognize that assault weapons,
however common, are unusually dangerous and that the
Second Amendment allows local governments to regulate
such weapons.
A. The Second Amendment allows governments
to restrict unusually dangerous weapons.
In District of Columbia v. Heller , 554 U.S. 570, 596
(2008), this Court confirmed that the Second Amendment
does not “protect the right of citizens to carry arms for
any sort of confrontation.” Implicit in that statement was
the fact that weapons of war or those used largely by
criminals for malevolent purposes—such as the machine
guns and sawed-off shotguns regulated by the National
Firearms Act of 1934—are not within Second Amendment
protections. Accordingly, this Court explained that the
Second Amendment’s scope is not unlimited and that
“dangerous and unusual” weapons that were not “in
common use at the time” may be regulated. Id. at 627.
Lower courts differ in deciding what constitutes
“dangerous and unusual” weapons that can be regulated,
with some treating the common law phrase as if it contains
conjunctive statutory elements, requiring a weapon to
be both dangerous and unusual, while others interpret
the phrase to mean “unusually dangerous.” History and
tradition advise that an “unusually dangerous” weapon
may be regulated and that regulation is not prohibited
simply because such a weapon is owned in large numbers.

5
1. The historic phrases “dangerous and
unusual” and “dangerous or unusual” are
best understood to mean weapons that are
“unusually dangerous.”
Historical prohibitions of “dangerous and unusual”
weapons are best understood as prohibitions on unusually
dangerous weapons. This formulation is consistent with
the Nation’s history and tradition of weapon regulation,
gives independent meaning to the word “dangerous,” and
better aligns with the purpose of the Second Amendment.
Rather than focusing on a weapon’s commonality, it allows
governments to consider whether a weapon’s destructive
capacity is disproportionate to the lawful self-defense
purpose the Second Amendment protects.
The historic use of the phrase “dangerous and
unusual” confirms rather than defeats this understanding.
Recognizing an “important limitation on the right to keep
and carry arms,” Heller relied on common-law sources
on the law of affray. 554 U.S. at 627; see also  1 William
Hawkins, A Treatise of the Pleas of the Crown  135
(1716) (explaining an affray occurs “where a Man arms
himself with dangerous and unusual Weapons, in such a
Manner as will naturally cause a Terror to the People”);
see also  4 William Blackstone, Commentaries on the
Laws of England  1 48-4 9  ( 1 7 69 )  ( “Th e  o ff e n c e  o f  ri din g
or going armed, with dangerous or unusual weapons, is
a crime against the public peace, by terrifying the good
people of the land”). While those common-law sources
concerned carrying weapons, Heller  applied them to
describe weapons subject to restriction under the Second
Amendment generally. Underlying these restrictions was
the principle that threats to public safety justified certain

6
limits on the right to keep and bear arms. Thus, the
common-law sources relied on in Heller reflect a historical
tradition of regulating weapons presenting an exceptional
danger to the public.
Notably, Heller cited twelve historical sources to
support the proposition that there is a “historical tradition
of prohibiting the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual
weapons.’” 554 U.S. at 627.  Six of the twelve used the
phrase “dangerous or unusual” rather than “dangerous
and unusual.” 2 Since Heller, one view is that arms must
be both “dangerous” and “unusual” to be regulable. See,
e.g., Caetano v. Massachusetts , 577 U.S. 411, 417 (2016)
(Alito, J., concurring); VanDerStok v. Garland , 86 F .4th
179, 184 n.6 (5th Cir. 2023). As noted above, however, the
historical sources Heller r e li e d  o n  d o  n o t  s u p p o rt  th e
conjunctive reading.
Moreover, reading “dangerous and unusual”
conjunctively gives no meaning to “dangerous” because
all weapons are inherently dangerous. “Dangerous” would
become surplusage and “unusual” would do all the work.
If “dangerous” means only the ordinary dangerousness
inherent in all firearms, then “dangerous and unusual”
functionally becomes “unusual” alone.
Instead, “dangerous and unusual” is best understood
as a hendiadys,  a  fi gur e  o f  s p e e c h  u s in g  “tw o  te rm s
separated by a conjunction [that] work together as a
single complex expression.” Samuel Bray, “Necessary
2. Joseph Blocher, The Common Use Test and the Question
of Constitutional Coverage , mich. l. rev. (forthcoming 2027)
(manuscript at 19), https://ssrn.com/abstract=7035841

7
and Proper” and “Cruel and Unusual”: Hendiadys in
the Constitution , 102 Va. L. Rev. 687, 688 (2016). As a
hendiadys, both “dangerous and unusual” and “dangerous
or unusual” mean “unusually dangerous.” Nat’l Ass’n for
Gun Rts. v. Lamont, 153 F .4th 213, 252 n.19 (2d Cir. 2025).
This “unusually dangerous” interpretation is consistent
with the historical sources on which Heller relies and
results in a more workable standard for defining the
Second Amendment’s scope.
Some circuits have interpreted “dangerous and
unusual” this way. The Fourth Circuit reasoned that
the relevant consideration is a weapon’s “ability to inflict
damage on a scale or in a manner disproportionate to the
end of personal protection.” Bianchi v. Brown , 111 F.4th
438, 451 (4th Cir. 2024) (en banc). Similarly, the Second
Circuit concluded that “historical tradition encompasses
those arms that legislators determined were unusually
dangerous because of their characteristics.” Lamont, 153
F .4th at 233; see also Hanson v. District of Columbia 120
F .4th 223, 238 n.7 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (reading “dangerous and
unusual” to mean “uncommonly dangerous”); Barnett v.
Raoul, 180 F .4th 1035, 1046 (7th Cir. 2026) (recognizing
a historical tradition of restrictions on “particularly
dangerous weapons”). These courts interpret the phrase
as the historical sources suggest—permitting restrictions
on unusually dangerous weapons—rather than treating
“dangerous” and “unusual” as independent requirements.
The Nation’s history of weapon regulations supports
this interpretation. In the Nineteenth century, bowie knives
and the like were subject to strict regulation because of
their uniquely dangerous qualities. See Cockrum v. State,
24 Tex. 394, 402-03 (1859) (describing bowie knives as “the

8
instrument of almost certain death”); Aymette v. State, 21
Tenn. 154 (1840) (permitting restrictions on bowie knives
because they are “dangerous to the peace and safety of the
citizens”). Twentieth century firearm restrictions support
the same conclusion. The National Firearms Act of 1934,
which regulated ownership and registration of machine
guns and short-barreled shotguns, was passed after those
weapons became popular with “the mass shooters of their
day.” Ocean State Tactical, LLC v. Rhode Island, 95 F.4th
38, 47 (1st Cir. 2024). Such restrictions arose because of the
especially dangerous nature of the weapons, not because
they were independently dangerous and unusual.
The unusually dangerous approach also better
accounts for technological developments. The Second
Amendment is not “trapped in amber,” its scope
confined to regulations in existence in 1791. United
States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680, 691 (2024). Just as
the Constitutional protection may account for modern
developments, so too should the historical tradition of
regulation account for developments that increase a
weapon’s destructive capacity. To hold otherwise would
permit technological advancements to expand the Second
Amendment’s protections while simultaneously restricting
governmental power to regulate the very dangers such
advancements create. The unusually dangerous approach
prevents this imbalance by allowing local governments to
respond to modern developments in weapon technology
with regulations consistent with the Nation’s historical
tradition of regulating particularly dangerous weapons.
The unusually dangerous standard provides a
more workable framework for delineating the Second
Amendment. This Court has recognized that “individual

9
self-defense is the central component of the Second
Amendment right.” New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n,
Inc. v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1, 29 (2022) (internal citations
omitted). The unusually dangerous standard protects
the right to armed self-defense while still preserving
the governmental power to regulate weapons whose
destructive capacities far exceed that purpose in a
particular community.
2. The Court should not decide whether
the Second Amendment guarantees
possession of a particular firearm based
on how many of them currently exist.
Some equate whether a weapon is dangerous and
unusual to whether the weapon is in “common use.” See
Duncan v. Bonta , 133 F .4th 852, 903 (9th Cir. 2025)
(Bumatay, J., dissenting) (noting that whether a weapon
is dangerous and unusual or in common use are “different
sides of the same coin”). An analysis asking only whether a
weapon is in common use ignores the origin of the phrase
“common use” in Second Amendment case law, fails to
account for differences across the Nation, and creates a
test that is simultaneously both over- and under-inclusive
of Second Amendment protections.
The genesis of “common use” is United States v.
Miller, 307 U.S. 174 (1939), where the Court explained
that “ordinarily when called for service [militia] men
were expected to appear bearing arms supplied by
themselves and of the kind in common use at the time .”
Id. at 179 (emphasis added). Though noting that Miller
was “virtually unreasoned,” Heller relied on its passing
reference to “common use at the time.” 554 U.S. at 624

10
n.24. Quoting Miller, Heller  stated that the types of
weapons within the Second Amendment’s scope were those
“in common use at the time.” Id. at 627. But Miller did not
purport to prescribe a test for determining the Second
Amendment’s scope; it made a historical observation about
militia service. Miller’s inquiry was historical, examining
arms used by militiamen at the time of the founding, but
Petitioners argue that the common use inquiry considers
the contemporary prevalence of a weapon. Heller should
not be understood to transform a passing historical
observation from Miller in to  a  c o n s ti tu ti o n al  s tan d ar d
for all time.
Some courts rely on circulation and ownership data
to apply a common use test, but that approach ensures
that “what can be banned depends on what has been
banned.” Barnett, 180 F .4th at 1074. The approach thus
produces “absurd results.” Del. State Sportsmen’s Ass’n
v. Del. Dep’t of Safety & Homeland Security , 108 F .4th
194, 213 (3d Cir. 2024) (Roth, J., concurring). For example,
the Federal Assault Weapons Ban of 1994 prohibited the
manufacture, transfer, and possession of certain AR-15
style rifles produced after the act’s effective date. Public
Safety and Recreational Firearms Use Protection Act,
Pub. L. No. 103-322, 108 Stat. 1996 (1994). At the time it
went into effect, few civilians owned AR-15s. Del. State
Sportsmen’s Ass’n, 108 F .4th at 213 (Roth, J., concurring).
When the ban expired in 2004, AR-15s “began to occupy a
more significant share of the market.” Id. Looking only at
circulation and ownership data, the ban would have been
constitutional before 2004 and then would have become
unconstitutional at some point thereafter. Id. The scope
of a constitutional right should not “be contingent on the
results of a popularity contest.” Id.

11
Additionally, reliance on ownership data imposes on
cities standards that are better suited for rural areas. The
D.C. Circuit has reasoned that the relevant geographical
area for a common use inquiry is the entire United States
because “[i]t would be anomalous for the protection offered
by the Second Amendment to vary from one state or place
to another based upon the local popularity of a particular
firearm.” Hanson, 120 F.4th at 232. But it is not clear why
that calculus would be anomalous. Historically, densely
populated areas were permitted to tailor arms regulations
to respond to dangers unique to those areas. The statute
of Northampton provided that no man shall “ride armed
by night nor by day, in Fairs or Markets .” Statute of
Northampton, 1328, 2 Edw. 3, c. 3 (Eng.) (emphasis added).
And restrictions on travel and storage of gunpowder in
the eighteenth century were enacted to protect growing
population centers such as Boston, Philadelphia, and
New York City. Saul Cornell & Nathan DeDino, A Well
Regulated Right: The Early American Origins of Gun
Control, 73 Fordham L. Rev. 487, 510-11 (2004). Cities
should not lose their ability to protect the public simply
because a weapon is widely owned elsewhere.
Along with the difficulty of defining “common,” a
common use inquiry risks being both over- and underinclusive. On one hand, a common use test based on
ownership would allow the government to act quickly when
a new arm is developed to prevent it from ever becoming
common, which would be over-inclusive. See Heller, 554
U.S. at 721 (Breyer, J., dissenting).
On the other hand, a common use test might protect
newly-developed arms that are unusually dangerous,
giving the government no opportunity to act, which

12
would be under-inclusive. Blocher, supra  (manuscript
at 49-50). Imagine that a company develops a popular
app that makes cellphones capable of emitting a painful
or deadly sound. The phones would then be “arms” as
Heller defines them, but the government would have no
opportunity to ban the app. Id. The apps could become “in
common use” virtually overnight and possession under the
Second Amendment would be guaranteed. Id. Thus, as
technological innovation outpaces regulation, the common
use test risks placing unusually dangerous weapons
beyond the reach of regulation before governments have
any meaningful opportunity to respond.
As the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops
contends, “the commercial proliferation of a weapon
before it is regulated should not constitute an automatic
constitutional immunization from regulation in the future.”
Brief for the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops
as Amicus Curiae in Support of Neither Party at 21.
A common use test provides a shaky foundation for
the Second Amendment’s scope. It lacks a clear definition
of “common,” produces absurd results, and can lead to
both over- and under-inclusion. Resolution of Second
Amendment claims should instead focus on whether
a weapon is unusually dangerous; that is, whether its
ability to inflict damage is disproportionate to its lawful
ends. This approach better comports with the Second
Amendment’s purpose while avoiding the arbitrary
consequences of an inquiry based on prevalence.

B. Assault weapons are unusually dangerous.
Assault weapons are unusually dangerous, based on
their origin, their use in mass shootings, and their effects
on law enforcement.
1. Their origin shows they are unusually
dangerous.
Combining rapid fire, large ammunition capacity,
and high-velocity rounds, assault weapons are uniquely
capable of mass casualties. Assault weapons such as the
AR-15 were created after World War II for the United
States military. Kolbe v. Hogan, 849 F.3d 114, 124-25 (4th
Cir. 2017) (en banc), abrogated on other grounds by N.Y.
State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022). The
Army found AR-15s to be superior to M-14s, a comparable
military assault rifle then in use. Id. at 125. In the Vietnam
War, American soldiers were equipped with AR-15s, and
then the Department of Defense purchased more than
100,000 AR-15s for the Army and the Air Force, changing
their name from “AR-15” to “M16.” Id. The intertwined
origins of AR-15s and M16s show that these weapons were
intended for military use, not individual self-defense. See
e.g., Bianchi , 111 F .4th at 454; Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rts.
v. Lamont, 685 F . Supp. 3d 63, 101 (D. Conn. 2023), aff’d,
153 F .4th 213 (2d Cir. 2025).
AR-15s and other assault weapons are “semiautomatic
versions of machineguns initially designed for military
use.” Kolbe, 849 F.3d at 125. Automatic machineguns fire
the ammunition in a large-capacity thirty-round magazine
within approximately two seconds. Id. Semiautomatic

14
weapons can fire ammunition from the same capacity
magazine within approximately five seconds. Id.
The similarities include more than firing speed. AR-
15s use the same internal piston firing system and use
the same ammunition that leaves the muzzle at a similar
velocity, travels a similar distance, and delivers a similar
amount of kinetic energy on impact. See Bianchi, 111 F.4th
at 454-55. AR-15 assault weapons, like the M16, use 20- or
30-round magazines with compatibility up to 100-round
magazines. Id. at 455. Both weapons can be equipped with
a number of combat-focused features. Id. Be y o n d th eir
military-focused design, assault weapons can be enhanced
through devices such as a “forced reset trigger,” which
enables a user to achieve machine-gun-like rates of fire,
and bump stocks, an assault weapon accessory that “allows
the shooter to rapidly reengage the trigger.” 3

Petitioners would set this all aside as post-ratification.
Pet. Br. 46. But Bruen held only that later practice cannot
“overcome or alter” an inconsistent original meaning. 597
U.S. at 36. Bruen did not make a consistent later practice
irrelevant to confirming what earlier enactments show.
These charters contradict nothing in the Founding-era
record. Rather, they continue it. Sovereigns that confer
the same power on town after town for four generations
were recognizing where power to regulate resided.
Municipal corporations are, after all, “convenient agencies
for exercising such of the governmental powers of the
state as may be [e]ntrusted to them.” Hunter v. City of
Pittsburgh, 207 U.S. 161, 178 (1907).
Petitioners’ principal response is that under Heller
the historical record need not be consulted at all. In their
view, Heller reduced the historical inquiry for arms to a
single question, whether the weapon is “in common use,” so
that “there is no need for fresh historical analysis because
Heller  alr e ad y  h as  s e t  th e  his to ri cal  gr o un d  rul e s . ”
Pet. Br. 24; see id. at 28-29. But in Heller the Court
expressly declined to “undertake an exhaustive historical
analysis . . . of the full scope of the Second Amendment.”
554 U.S. at 626. The Court cautioned that its first in-depth

28
examination of the right should not be expected “to clarify
the entire field.” Id. at 635. Its common-use language
was a conclusion drawn from history, a limitation “fairly
supported by the historical tradition,” not a substitute for
that history. Id. at 627. The tradition Petitioners decline
to consult is there. It is written in the ordinances of towns
and in the charters that empowered them, and it holds
that the governments nearest a danger may act against it.
2. The police power is a trust committed to
state and local governments for the safety
of communities.
It is well-established that “the power of governing is
a trust committed by the people to the government, no
part of which can be granted away.” Stone v. Mississippi,
101 U.S. 814, 820 (1880). Through our Constitution, the
Founders denied the federal government this police
power; it is instead “reposed in the States.” United States
v. Morrison , 529 U.S. 598, 618 (2000). “Public safety,
public health, morality, peace and quiet, law and order—
these are some of the more conspicuous examples of the
traditional application of the police power to municipal
affairs.” Berman v. Parker , 348 U.S. 26, 32 (1954).
Throughout their history, state and local governments
“have exercised their police powers to protect the health
and safety of their citizens.” Medtronic, Inc. v. Lohr, 518
U.S. 470, 475 (1996).
This Court has repeatedly recognized that a central
responsibility of state and local government is “protecting
the health, safety, and welfare of its citizens.” United
Haulers Ass’n v. Oneida-Herkimer Solid Waste Mgmt.
Auth., 550 U.S. 330, 342 (2007); see also Metro. Life Ins.

29
Co. v. Massachusetts, 471 U.S. 724, 756 (1985) (“The
States traditionally have had great latitude under their
police powers to legislate as to the protection of the
lives, limbs, health, comfort, and quiet of all persons.”).
A Second Amendment interpretation that prohibits local
governments from regulating assault weapons does
precisely the opposite: what should be a question for state
and local governments to debate and decide to protect
their citizens is instead improperly removed from their
sphere.
“[T]he Constitution establishes a federal republic
where local differences are cherished as elements of
liberty, rather than eliminated in a search for national
uniformity.” Friedman v. City of Highland Park, 784 F .3d
406, 412 (7th Cir. 2015), cert. denied , 577 U.S. 1039 (2015)
(relying in part on federalism to hold that a city’s assault
weapon ban did not violate the Second Amendment).
James Madison echoes this principle in The Federalist
No. 39: “local or municipal authorities form distinct and
independent portions of the supremacy, no more subject,
within their respective spheres, to the general authority,
than the general authority is subject to them, within its
own sphere.” State and local governments are meant
to have distinct and independent powers to protect and
promote the safety of their citizens—but Petitioners ask
the Court to curtail these powers.
Local governments have raised this concern before
and received assurances that “local experimentation
with reasonable firearms regulations will continue
under the Second Amendment.” McDonald v. City of
Chicago, 561 U.S. 742, 784-85 (2010). In McDonald, the
municipal respondents argued that incorporating the

30
Second Amendment would disable local governments from
addressing conditions peculiar to their communities. Id.
at 783-84. The Court did not reply that federalism has no
place in this area. The Court stated that a fundamental
guarantee “limits (but by no means eliminates) their
ability to devise solutions to social problems that suit
local needs and values,” and that “[d]espite municipal
respondents’ doomsday proclamations, incorporation does
not imperil every law regulating firearms.” Id. at 785-86.
Heller similarly stated that while “the enshrinement
of constitutional rights necessarily takes certain policy
choices off the table,” “[t]he Constitution leaves the
District of Columbia a variety of tools for combating”
handgun violence. 554 U.S. at 636. Those assurances
answered precisely the concern amici raise here, and local
governments have legislated in reliance on them for over
fifteen years. And the greater dangers assault weapons
impose on society should ensure local governments a
greater “variety of tools” for combating assault weapon
violence.
Legislatures do not pass assault weapon regulations
in a vacuum, and that is especially evident in the
cases consolidated before this Court. For Connecticut,
the General Assembly made its legislative judgment
concerning assault weapons after the tragic mass-shooting
at Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012. Cuomo, 804
F .3d at 248. For Cook County, there have been various
ordinances in place banning the possession of assault
weapons since 1993. Wilson v. Cnty. of Cook, 968 N.E.2d
641, 645 (Ill. 2012). These ordinances were passed due
to “easy access to firearms and ammunition” becoming
“a concern of public health, safety and welfare for the

31
citizens of Cook County” and due to assault weapons being
“20 times more likely to be used in the commission of a
crime than other kinds of weapons.” Id. Both Connecticut
and Cook County’s assault weapon bans were legislative
judgments made for the purpose of promoting public
safety. That distinction is particularly important because
the work of public safety falls overwhelmingly on cities
and counties.
3. Local governments respond to, and bear
the cost of, mass shootings.
When mass shootings occur, local governments are
closest to the harm and bear the heaviest costs.47 Consider
for a moment everything that a shooting sets in motion.
As members of the public see and respond to the shooting,
their calls go to a public safety answering point operated
by a city or a county.48 A dispatcher sends officers from a
municipal police department or a county sheriff’s office.
Paramedics arrive from a local fire department or a county
emergency medical service, and a fire crew secures the
scene. If the shooting happened at a school, a locally
elected board closes the building, and district counselors

in a park or near a public space, a municipal department

The ambulance, which is provided by the local
government, carries the wounded to a hospital that
in many communities is operated by the state or local
government. If victims die, a county medical examiner
performs the autopsies and notifies the families. 49 City
or county detectives investigate, and evidence goes to a
county laboratory. A county prosecutor charges the case,
a county public defender answers it, and any pretrial
detention happens in a county jail. Following the shooting,
the local city council or county board that funds every
one of these functions will face its residents at the next
public meeting.
Beyond these immediate impacts, mass shootings
have been found to reduce employment in the affected
county by roughly 1.3%, with lasting effects on earnings
and housing prices. Abel Brodeur & Hasin Yousaf, On
the Economic Consequences of Mass Shootings , 107 Rev.
Econ. & Stat. 109, 112 (2025).
Based on all these local effects, it is unsurprising
that when this Court has reviewed firearm regulations,
the challenged acts have often been municipal. See, e.g.,
McDonald, 561 U.S. at 750 (reviewing Chicago’s handgun
ordinance); Heller, 554 U.S. at 574-75 (2008) (the same

The governments involved at nearly every step before
and after a shooting are the governments Petitioners
ask this Court to curtail. They are the governments that
all Americans continue to hold in high esteem: Pew has
found that 63% of Republicans and 64% of Democrats
hold a favorable view of their local government, against
11% and 32% respectively for the federal government. 50
Gallup has similarly found that trust in local government
has remained between 66% and 73% since the 1970s, and
above 60% in every political affiliation in every decade,
even as trust in the federal government to handle domestic
problems fell from 70% to 38%. 51
Whatever has become of Americans’ confidence in
more distant institutions, the local forum is one that
citizens of both parties still credit and still use. A county
board meeting is a forum an ordinary resident can attend
on a weeknight. Thus, whenever a constitutional rule
forbids local governments from acting, it removes the

act in the aftermath of the next mass shootings whatever
